title.en: The Origin of the Human Race: Sky Holder Brings Out the Six Pairs
title.zh: 人類之起源：天主攜六對而出

region.en: State of New York (the six tribal homes), symbolic pin at Onondaga, the council fire
region.zh: 紐約州（六族故地），象徵性定位於擁有議火之奧農達加

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. IV: 'Origin of the human race'

summary.en: Deep water covers the earth; ducks in council receive with overlapping pinions a beautiful woman falling from the sky, and the giant tortoise volunteers to hold her, growing into an island. Twin boys are born - one the spirit of good who makes the maize, fruit and tobacco grow, one the spirit of evil who creates the weeds and vermin - and the world still quakes with the tortoise's stretching. Ages later Sky Holder (Ta-rhun-hia-wah-kun) brings six pairs from the bosom of the great island: Mohawk by the great river, Oneida by the big stone, Onondaga on the high hill, the Tuscarora carried up the Roanoke into North Carolina - each tribe claiming it was the favored one, the Onondagas proving it by their council fire.
summary.zh: 深水覆地；群鴨聚議，以層層羽翼承接自天而降的美女，巨龜自願負她於背，身軀漸長成島。婦人誕下雙生——一為善靈，令玉米果實菸草生長；一為惡靈，造出莠草害蟲——大地至今因巨龜伸展而震動。多年之後，天主教主（塔爾洪尼亞瓦岡）自大島懷中攜出六對人：莫霍克居大河之畔，奧奈達居巨石之側，奧農達加居高丘，塔斯卡洛拉被攜往洛亞諾克河上游而至北卡羅來納——各族皆自稱蒙選，而奧農達加以議火為證。

sensitivity.note: Smith's synthesis of Cayuga-Seneca-Tuscarora tellings (1883); public domain. She notes the twins' good/evil wording is likely a modern framing.

passages.text: In the great past, deep water covered all the earth. The air was filled with birds, and great monsters were in possession of the waters, when a beautiful woman was seen by them falling from the sky. Then huge ducks gathered in council and resolved to meet this wonderful creature and break the force of her fall. So they arose, and, with pinion overlapping pinion, unitedly received the dusky burden. Then the monsters of the deep also gathered in council to decide which should hold this celestial being and protect her from the terrors of the water, but none was able except a giant tortoise, who volunteered to endure this lasting weight upon his back. There she was gently placed, while he, constantly increasing in size, soon became a large island.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

passages.text: Twin boys were after a time brought forth by the woman - one the spirit of good, who made all good things, and caused the maize, fruit, and tobacco to grow; the other the spirit of evil, who created the weeds and all vermin. Ever the world was increasing in size, although occasional quakings were felt, caused by the efforts of the monster tortoise to stretch out, or by the contraction of his muscles. After the lapse of ages from the time of his general creation Ta-rhun-hia-wah-kun, the Sky Holder, resolved upon a special creation of a race which should surpass all others in beauty, strength, and bravery; so from the bosom of the great island, where they had previously subsisted upon moles, Ta-rhun-hia-wah-kun brought out the six pairs, which were destined to become the greatest of all people.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

passages.text: The first pair were left near a great river, now called the Mohawk; the second by the side of a big stone - the Oneidas; another on a high hill - the Onondagas. Each pair was left with careful instructions in different parts of what is now the State of New York, except the Tuscaroras, who were taken up the Roanoke River into North Carolina, where Ta-rhun-hia-wah-kun also took up his abode, teaching them many useful arts before his departure. Each of the six tribes will tell you that his own was the favored one with whom Sky Holder made his terrestrial home, while the Onondagas claim that their possession of the council fire proves them to have been the chosen people. As the numerous families became scattered over the State, some lived where the bear was the principal game and were called the clan of the Bear; others where the beavers were trapped - the Beaver clan; and for similar reasons the Snipe, Deer, Wolf, Tortoise, and Eel clans received their appellations.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

title.en: The Fat Turtle Who Became the Progenitor of the Turtle Clan

region.en: Small lake or pool in the early Iroquois country
region.zh: 早期易洛魁之地的小湖

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. IV: 'Formation of the Turtle Clan'

summary.en: In a hot summer a pool of mud turtles dries up, and the turtles set out across the country for a new habitation. One particularly fat turtle suffers so from the exercise that his shoulders blister under his shell until, by an extraordinary effort, he throws off his shell altogether; the transformation continues until the fat and lazy turtle becomes a man, the progenitor of the Turtle clan.
summary.zh: 炎夏之季，泥龜所在的小池乾涸，龜群遂跋涉遷居。其中一隻特別肥碩的龜因勞頓而肩胛在殼下起泡，終於奮力掙脫全身甲殼；蛻變之勢不停，這隻肥懶之龜化作人形，即為龜氏族之祖。

passages.text: There were in early times many tortoises of the kind familiarly known as mud turtles, inhabiting a small lake or pool. During a very hot summer this pool became dry. The turtles thereupon set out on their travels over the country to look for a new habitation. One of them, who was particularly fat, suffered a good deal from this unaccustomed exercise. After a time his shoulders became blistered under his shell from the effect of his exertions in walking, and he, finally, by an extraordinary effort, threw off his shell altogether. The process of transformation and development, thus commenced, went on, and in a short time this fat and lazy turtle became a man, who was the progenitor of the Turtle clan.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

title.en: How the Bear Lost His Tail: The Fox, the Fish, and the Duel
title.zh: 熊失尾記：狐狸、魚與決鬥

region.en: Six Nations Reserve, Grand River, Ontario (related by a grandchild of Brant)
region.zh: 加拿大安大略省格蘭德河六族保留地（布蘭特之孫講述）

texts.period: Related by Ka-an-er-wah, grandchild of the Mohawk Brant (Smith 1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. IV: 'How the bear lost his tail'

summary.en: A cunning fox feigns death by a fish-wagon road and is tossed aboard, throwing out fish until he crawls away. He advises a wolf to try the same trick - the fisherman, forewarned, thrashes him. To the bear he teaches the ice-fishing ruse: put your tail in the air-hole; the bear's tail freezes off. Challenged to a duel, the fox chooses a dog and a lame cat as seconds, the bear a hog; a squealing pig puts the whole company to flight, and the bear never avenges the loss of his tail.
summary.zh: 狡狐裝死於運魚車必經之路，被擲上車後丟魚而遁。牠教狼如法炮製——漁夫識破，把狼痛打一頓。又教熊以尾垂入冰洞釣魚；天寒，熊尾凍斷。熊怒而約決鬥；狐以犬與跛貓為助，熊以豬為助；豬受驚尖叫，全場潰逃，熊終未能報失尾之仇。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883 ('a modern Indian story'); public domain. European trickster-tale elements overlay an Iroquois frame.

passages.text: A cunning fox saw a wagon load of fish and resorted to the following ruse to obtain some of the coveted delicacy: feigning to be dead, he laid himself in the road by which the fisherman must pass, who, thinking the skin of the fox worth preserving, tossed him into his wagon and drove on. After throwing out several fish, the fox slyly crawled out himself. Soon he met a wolf who was informed of his good luck, and advised to try the same experiment; the fisherman had, in the mean time, discovered the trick, and the wolf received a good thrashing instead of a fish dinner.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

passages.text: The fox next met a bear who was also anxious to procure some fish. 'Well,' replied the fox, 'down at the river you will find an air-hole in the ice; just put your tail down into it as I did and you can draw out the fish as fast as you wish.' The bear followed the directions carefully, but, the weather being cold, instead of securing a fish his tail was frozen off. The bear was very angry and proposed to fight a duel with the fox. The fox chose as his seconds a dog and a cat; the bear chose a hog, and awaited the fox at the appointed hour.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

passages.text: As the latter was late in appearing the bear clambered into a tree to prospect, and reported that the fox was approaching with two men armed with guns; thereupon the hog, greatly frightened, begged to be covered with leaves. The fox soon made his appearance, but instead of men his companions proved to be a dog and a lame cat; while awaiting their turn, the cat, perceiving the slight motion of one of the uncovered ears of the hog, sprang upon it, whereupon the squeals of the invisible pig put the whole company to flight, and the bear never had the satisfaction of avenging the loss of his tail.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

title.en: The Sores-Covered Stranger and the Medicine of the Bear Clan

region.en: Village of clan-marked wigwams in the Iroquois country
region.zh: 易洛魁之地懸有族徽的村寨

texts.period: Related by Chief Mt. Pleasant of the Bear clan (Smith 1883)

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. IV: 'Origin of medicine'

summary.en: A sickly old man covered with sores goes from clan-marked wigwam to wigwam asking food and lodging, and is scorned by the Wolf, the Tortoise and the Heron. At the Bear-skin wigwam a kind-hearted woman feeds him and spreads skins; he directs her to gather and prepare certain herbs that heal him, then, fevered, other herbs, again and again - until he tells his benefactress her mission is accomplished and she is endowed with all the secrets of curing disease. A hemlock tree shall grow above all others before her wigwam, signifying the Bear's precedence, and she and her clan shall increase and multiply.
summary.zh: 一位滿身癩瘡的老人逐一叩乞各氏族之屋，遭狼、龜、鷺之族鄙視驅趕。至熊皮之屋，善心婦人供食鋪皮；老人教她採製諸藥，治癒己身——屢病屢教——直至言明：其使命已畢，婦人已得醫治百病之秘。屋前將生一株高出群木的鐵杉，為熊族居首之徵，婦人及其族人將繁衍興旺。

passages.text: Chief Mt. Pleasant, one of the Bear clan, relates that once on a time a sickly old man, covered with sores, entered an Indian village where over each wigwam was placed the sign of the clan of its possessor; for instance, the beaver skin denoting the Beaver clan, the deer skin the Deer clan. At each of these wigwams the old man applied for food and a night's lodging, but his repulsive appearance rendered him an object of scorn, and the Wolf, the Tortoise, and the Heron had bidden the abject old man to pass on. At length, tired and weary, he arrived at a wigwam where a bear skin betokened the clanship of its owner, inhabited by a kind-hearted woman who immediately refreshed him with food and spread out skins for his bed.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

passages.text: Then she was instructed by the old man to go in search of certain herbs, which she prepared according to his directions, and through their efficacy he was soon healed. Then he commanded that she should treasure up this secret. A few days after, he sickened with a fever and again commanded a search for other herbs and was again healed. This being many times repeated, he at last told his benefactress that his mission was accomplished, and that she was now endowed with all the secrets for curing disease in all its forms, and that before her wigwam should grow a hemlock tree whose branches should reach high into the air above all others, to signify that the Bear should take precedence of all other clans, and that she and her clan should increase and multiply.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

title.en: The Origin of Tobacco: The Burned Boat of Medicine Men
title.zh: 菸草之起源：焚燒的醫者之舟

region.en: River bank of the Iroquois country

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. IV: 'Origin of tobacco'

summary.en: A loud voice proclaims that all must remain indoors as a boat of medicine men passes the river bank; some disobey and die immediately. The boat is found next day with a strange being asleep at each end, and the voice declares that destroying these creatures will be a great blessing to the Indian. They are decoyed into a neighboring council-house, put to death and burned - and from their ashes rises the tobacco plant.
summary.zh: 醫者之舟行經河岸之際，巨聲宣告眾人須閉戶不出；違者立即斃命。翌日尋得該舟，兩端各睡著一位奇異之人；巨聲再言：誅此二物，將大有益於印第安人。眾人誘其入鄰近議屋，殺而焚之——菸草之株自其灰燼中長出。

passages.text: A boat filled with medicine men passed near a river bank, where a loud voice had proclaimed to all the inhabitants to remain indoors; but some, disobeying, died immediately. The next day the boat was sought for and found, containing a strange being at each end, both fast asleep. A loud voice was then heard saying that the destroying of these creatures would result in a great blessing to the Indian. So they were decoyed into a neighboring council-house, where they were put to death and burned, and from their ashes rose the tobacco plant.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

title.en: The Origin of Plumage: The Turkey-Buzzard's Selfish Choice
title.zh: 羽衣之起源：兀鷲的自私擇衣

region.en: The birds' first council ground (symbolic pin in the Genesee valley)
region.zh: 群鳥最初的議事地（象徵性定位於傑納西河谷）

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. IV: 'Origin of plumage'

summary.en: Created naked, the birds hide in shame until they petition the gods for covering; the garments lie far off, and each bird has an excuse - until the turkey-buzzard volunteers. On the long journey he is obliged to eat carrion and filth (hence his nature), and finds the coverings, selfishly trying on the most beautifully colored suit - but unable to fly in it - before choosing the least beautiful in which he rides so gracefully through the air. He then returns bearing the feathery garments, from which each bird chooses his present colored suit.
summary.zh: 群鳥初生赤裸，羞而匿藏，終向眾神請求衣裳；衣在遠方，諸鳥各有推辭，直至兀鷲自告奮勇。長途之上，牠（原本潔淨）被迫食腐啖穢，因而成了今日的兀鷲。尋得羽衣後，牠自私地先試最美的一件，卻不能飛；最後選定最樸素者——卻能翩然翔空。牠攜羽衣而歸，眾鳥各自擇得如今的彩衣。

passages.text: In the beginning the birds, having been created naked, remained hidden, being ashamed of their nakedness. But at last they assembled in a great council and petitioned the gods to give them some kind of covering. They were told that their coverings were all ready, but were a long way off, and they must either go or send for them. Accordingly, another council was held to induce some bird to go in search of the plumage, but each had some excuse for not going. At last a turkey-buzzard volunteered to go and bring the feathery uniforms.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

passages.text: It being a long journey to the place whence he must bring them, he (who had been a clean bird heretofore) was obliged to eat carrion and filth of all kinds; hence his present nature. At length, directed by the gods, he found the coverings, and selfishly appropriated to himself the most beautifully colored one, but finding he could not fly in this, he continued trying them on until he selected his present suit, in which, although it is the least beautiful of any, he can so gracefully ride through the air. The good turkey-buzzard then returned, bearing the feathery garments, from which each bird chose his present colored suit.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

title.en: Why the Chipmunk Has the Black Stripe on His Back

region.en: The animals' assembly at the hollow-tree holes
region.zh: 群獸聚於空心樹洞之會

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. IV: 'Why the chipmunk has the black stripe on his back'

summary.en: The porcupine, appointed leader of all the animals, calls the assembly to decide: shall there be night all the time, or daylight with its sunshine? The chipmunk sings 'The light will come; we must have light' while the bear sings 'Night is best; we must have darkness.' As the day dawns the chipmunk prevails; the enraged bear pursues him, and the huge paw, grazing his back as he enters his hole in a hollow tree, leaves the black imprint the chipmunk has ever since retained. But night and day have ever continued to alternate.
summary.zh: 豪豬奉命為群獸之長，召集眾獸議決：長夜無晝，抑或有日照之光明？花栗鼠唱「光明將至，我們要有光明」，熊則唱「黑夜最好，我們要有黑暗」。天將破曉，花栗鼠漸佔上風；暴怒的熊追之，巨掌在花栗鼠竄入空心樹洞之際擦過其背，留下至今的黑紋。而黑夜與白晝，自此永恆交替。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. A day/night dualism debate, rare in world aitiology.

passages.text: Once upon a time the porcupine was appointed to be the leader of all the animals. Soon after his appointment he called them all together and presented the question, 'Shall we have night all the time and darkness, or daylight with its sunshine?' This was a very important question, and a violent discussion arose, some wishing for daylight and the sun to rule, and others for continual night.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

passages.text: The chipmunk wished for night and day, weeks and months, and night to be separate from the days, so he began singing, 'The light will come; we must have light,' which he continued to repeat. Meanwhile the bear began singing, 'Night is best; we must have darkness.' While the chipmunk was singing, the day began to dawn. Then the other party saw that the chipmunk was prevailing, and were very angry; and their leader, the bear, pursued the chipmunk, who managed to escape uninjured, the huge paw of the bear simply grazing his back as he entered his hole in a hollow tree, leaving its black imprint, which the chipmunk has ever since retained. But night and day have ever continued to alternate.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

title.en: The Origin of the Constellations: Pleiades, Bear Chase, Old Man, and Moon Woman
title.zh: 星座之起源：昂宿、逐熊、老人與月娘

region.en: The night sky over the Iroquois country (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 易洛魁之地的夜空（象徵性定位）

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. IV: 'Origin of the constellations'

summary.en: Seven little boys denied their feast-dance supplies whirl off into the air around their singer and become the Pleiades, his brightness dimmed by homesickness. Hunters pursuing a bear are attacked by a monster stone giant; three survivors and the bear are carried by invisible spirits into the sky, where the first hunter aims his bow, the second carries the kettle, the third gathers sticks - and only in fall do the arrows pierce the bear, when his dripping blood tinges the autumn foliage. A despised old man sings his death chant up a high mountain and becomes Na-ge-tci, the old man; and a divining old woman, unhappy that she cannot foretell the end of the world, is transported to the moon, where she weaves a forehead-strap forever, her work unravelled monthly by the cat at her side.
summary.zh: 七個被拒絕宴舞食物的小男孩繞著歌者旋轉升空，化為昂宿星——歌者因思鄉而黯淡。獵熊者遭巨石巨人襲擊，三人與熊被無形精靈攜上天空：第一人張弓，第二人攜釜，第三人拾柴——唯有秋天獵箭能刺熊，其滴血染紅秋葉。受鄙夷的老人登高山唱死亡之歌而昇天，是為「老人」星；一位能卜卻算不出世界末日的老婦被移至月中，永遠編織額帶，身旁的貓每月拆散其網——故其工永不能畢。

sensitivity.note: Smith 1883; public domain. Smith assembles four star-aitia in one passage; cut here as one composite record.

passages.text: Iroquois tradition tells us that the sun and moon existed before the creation of the earth, but the stars had all been mortals or favored animals and birds. Seven little Indian boys were once accustomed to bring at eve their corn and beans to a little mound, upon the top of which, after their feast, the sweetest of their singers would sit and sing for his mates who danced around the mound. On one occasion they resolved on a more sumptuous feast, and each was to contribute towards a savory soup; but the parents refused them the needed supplies, and they met for a feastless dance. Their heads and hearts grew lighter as they flew around the mound, until suddenly the whole company whirled off into the air. The inconsolable parents called in vain for them to return; higher and higher they arose, whirling around their singer, until, transformed into bright stars, they took their places in the firmament, where, as the Pleiades, they are dancing still, the brightness of the singer having been dimmed, however, on account of his desire to return to earth.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

passages.text: A party of hunters were once in pursuit of a bear, when they were attacked by a monster stone giant, and all but three destroyed. The three together, with the bear, were carried by invisible spirits up into the sky, where the bear can still be seen, pursued by the first hunter with his bow, the second with the kettle, and the third, who, farther behind, is gathering sticks. Only in fall do the arrows of the hunters pierce the bear, when his dripping blood tinges the autumn foliage. Then for a time he is invisible, but afterwards reappears.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

passages.text: An old man, despised and rejected by his people, took his bundle and staff and went up into a high mountain, where he began singing the death chant. Those below, who were watching him, saw him slowly rise into the air, his chant ever growing fainter and fainter, until it finally ceased as he took his place in the heavens, where his stooping figure, staff, and bundle have ever since been visible, and are pointed out as Na-ge-tci (the old man). An old woman, gifted with the power of divination, was unhappy because she could not also foretell when the world would come to an end. For this she was transported to the moon, where to this day she is clearly to be seen weaving a forehead-strap. Once a month she stirs the boiling kettle of hominy before her, during which occupation the cat, ever by her side, unravels her net, and so she must continue until the end of time, for never until then will her work be finished.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

title.en: The Pole Star: Ti-yn-sou-da-go-err, the Star Which Never Moves

region.en: Territory of the pigmies, far north (symbolic pin on the Canadian Shield)
region.zh: 小人族之地，極北（象徵性定位於加拿大地盾）

source.work: Erminnie A. Smith, 'Myths of the Iroquois' (1883), ch. IV: 'The Pole Star'

summary.en: A migrating party, lost and famished by an unknown great river, holds council while their ill chief is tended. During the dance and burning tobacco a childlike being comes to guide them; by night she leads with only a small war-club, feasts them at dawn, and pours from a skin jug a draught that makes them feel very strong. Her own chief then arrives with a great number of his race: 'You are in the territory of the pigmies, who will teach you a sign, already in the sky, which will be a sure guide whenever you are lost' - and they point out the pole star, that in the north, where the sun never goes, stands still while other stars move. Following its light, the party reaches home, and the chief names the star ti-yn-sou-da-go-err, the star which never moves.
summary.zh: 遷徙的一族人迷失於無名大河之畔，飢餓瀕死，酋長病重。議會歌舞焚菸之際，一位孩童模樣的小人前來引路；她夜間僅持小杖領行，黎明備宴，並以皮囊倒出令眾人力大之感的神水。其族長率眾小人而至：「你們已入小人族之地。天空中已有一記號，迷路時可為你們的可靠指引。」眾小人指向北極星——在太陽永不到的北方，眾星移動，唯此星靜止。族人循星光歸家，大酋長召集諸族為此星命名「提恩蘇達戈爾」——永不移動之星。

passages.text: A large party of Indians, while moving in search of new hunting grounds, wandered on for many moons, finding but little game. At last they arrived at the banks of a great river, entirely unknown to them, where they had to stop, not having the material to build boats. Lost and nearly famished with hunger, the head chief was taken very ill, and it was decided to hold a council to devise means for returning to their old homes. During the dance, and while the tobacco was burning, a little being like a child came up, saying she was sent to be their guide. Accordingly they broke up their camp and started with her that night. Preceding them, with only a gi-wah, or small war-club, she led them on until daylight and then commanded them to rest while she prepared their food; when awakened by her they found a great feast in readiness for them.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

passages.text: At evening she reappeared, bringing with her a skin jug, from which she poured out some liquid into a horn cup, and bade them each to taste of it; at first they feared to do so, but yielding they began to feel very strong. She then informed them that they had a long journey to make that night, and in the early morn they arrived at a great plain. At night-fall she returned, saying her own chief would soon follow her to explain how they could reach their own homes in safety; in a short time he arrived, with a great number of his race, and immediately all held council together and informed the Indians that they were now in the territory of the pigmies, who would teach them a sign, already in the sky, which would be to them a sure guide whenever they were lost.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.

passages.text: The pigmies pointed out the pole star and told them that in the north, where the sun never goes, while other stars moved about, this particular star should stand still, as the Indian's guide in his wanderings; that they were then but to follow its light and they would soon return to their tribe, where they would find plenty of game. Then they thanked the good pigmies, and traveled every night until they arrived safely in their homes, where, when they had recounted all their adventures, the head chief called a meeting of all the tribes and said they ought to give this star a name. So they called it ti-yn-sou-da-go-err (the star which never moves), by which name it is called unto this day.
passages.note: Verbatim from Smith 1883, ch. IV; public domain.
